--- title: Scheduling Agents description: Run Hypertask agents on a schedule using any external scheduler â\x80\x94 GitHub Actions, crontab, Cloudflare Workers, or Vercel cron. --- Hypertask does not ship a built-in cron UI. It does not need one. Hypertask exposes a CLI and an MCP server, so any scheduler that can run a command on a schedule can trigger an agent run. This guide shows four common ways to schedule a recurring agent run. Pick the one that matches where your stack already lives. ## What "scheduled agent run" means A scheduled agent run is any workflow that: 1. Fires on a schedule (daily, weekly, every 15 minutes, etc.) 2. Invokes the `hypertask` CLI (or calls the MCP server directly) 3. Asks the agent to do something against your board â\x80\x94 triage inbox, post a daily standup, summarise last week's shipped tickets, auto-close stale bugs, etc. The agent runs, writes its result as a comment or a new task, and the scheduler moves on. No Hypertask-side cron engine is needed.
If you can write a one-liner shell command that does what you want, you can schedule it.
## Prerequisites You need: - The `hypertask` CLI installed on the machine (or runner) that will execute the schedule - A Hypertask API token â\x80\x94 export as `HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN` - A project ID to act on Install the CLI: ```bash npm install -g hypertask_cli ``` Verify: ```bash hypertask tasks list --project ``` ## Example 1 â\x80\x94 GitHub Actions Best for teams already on GitHub. Free for public repos, generous free tier for private. Create `.github/workflows/daily-standup.yml`: ```yaml name: Daily standup agent on: schedule: - cron: '0 8 * * 1-5' # 08:00 UTC, weekdays workflow_dispatch: # allow manual runs jobs: standup: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Install Hypertask CLI run: npm install -g hypertask_cli - name: Run standup agent env: HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN }} run: | hypertask tasks create \ --project 15 \ --title "Daily standup $(date -u +%Y-%m-%d)" \ --description "

Auto-generated by GitHub Actions. HyperAI, please summarise yesterday's shipped tickets.

" ``` Store the API token as a repository secret named `HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN`.
GitHub schedules are now bound to the repository's default branch. The schedule file on the default branch (production) is the one that fires each run. You no longer need a separate schedule copy on another branch.
## Example 2 â\x80\x94 crontab on a Linux server Best if you already have a VPS or home server running 24/7. Edit your crontab: ```bash crontab -e ``` Add: ```cron # Triage inbox every 15 minutes */15 * * * * /usr/bin/env HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN=xxxx hypertask tasks create --project 15 --title "Inbox triage" --description "HyperAI please scan the inbox and classify." # Weekly summary Mondays at 09:00 0 9 * * 1 /usr/bin/env HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN=xxxx hypertask tasks create --project 15 --title "Weekly summary" --description "HyperAI please summarise last week's wins." ``` Use a wrapper script instead of inline commands when they get longer than one line: ```bash #!/bin/bash # /home/you/hypertask-cron/weekly-summary.sh hypertask tasks create \ --project 15 \ --title "Weekly summary $(date -u +%Y-W%V)" \ --description "HyperAI please summarise last week's shipped tickets and flag any that are overdue." ``` Then in cron: ```cron 0 9 * * 1 /home/you/hypertask-cron/weekly-summary.sh ``` ## Example 3 â\x80\x94 Cloudflare Workers cron Best if you want zero-infra, run-anywhere scheduling and already use Cloudflare. Free tier covers 100k invocations per day. Create `wrangler.toml`: ```toml name = "hypertask-scheduler" main = "src/index.ts" compatibility_date = "2026-04-01" [triggers] crons = ["0 8 * * 1-5"] # 08:00 UTC weekdays ``` Create `src/index.ts`: ```ts async scheduled(_event: ScheduledEvent, env: Env) { const today = new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10); await fetch('https://app.hypertask.ai/api/tasks', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Authorization': `Bearer ${env.HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN}`, 'Content-Type': 'application/json', }, body: JSON.stringify({ projectId: 15, title: `Daily standup ${today}`, description: '

Auto-generated by Cloudflare Workers.

', }), }); }, }; interface Env { HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN: string; } ``` Deploy: ```bash wrangler secret put HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN wrangler deploy ```
Cloudflare Workers cron runs on Cloudflare's infrastructure, so you do not ship the Hypertask CLI to the worker. Call the HTTP endpoint directly or use the MCP server.
## Example 4 â\x80\x94 Vercel cron Best if your app already runs on Vercel. Free tier covers 2 cron jobs. Add to `vercel.json`: ```json { "crons": [ { "path": "/api/hypertask-standup", "schedule": "0 8 * * 1-5" } ] } ``` Create `pages/api/hypertask-standup.ts` (or `app/api/hypertask-standup/route.ts` for App Router): ```ts if (req.headers.authorization !== `Bearer ${process.env.CRON_SECRET}`) { return res.status(401).end(); } const today = new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10); await fetch('https://app.hypertask.ai/api/tasks', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Authorization': `Bearer ${process.env.HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN}`, 'Content-Type': 'application/json', }, body: JSON.stringify({ projectId: 15, title: `Daily standup ${today}`, description: '

Auto-generated by Vercel cron.

', }), }); res.status(200).json({ ok: true }); } ``` Set `HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN` and `CRON_SECRET` in the Vercel project environment variables. ## Common patterns Fire at 08:00 weekdays. Ask the agent to summarise what shipped yesterday and what is blocked. Posted as a new task in a "Standups" section. Fire every 15 minutes. Ask the agent to classify new inbox items (bug, feature, question, noise) and auto-archive noise. Fire weekly Sundays. Ask the agent to move any Backlog ticket untouched for 60 days into an "Archive" section. Fire Mondays at 09:00. Ask the agent to summarise last week's shipped tickets into a single "Weekly wins" task, for use in team updates or marketing. ## Choosing a scheduler | Scheduler | Use when | |---|---| | GitHub Actions | You already use GitHub and want CI-grade reliability. | | crontab | You have a VPS or home server running 24/7 and like full control. | | Cloudflare Workers | You want zero-infra scheduling at the edge. | | Vercel cron | Your app already runs on Vercel and you want crons living next to your routes. | ## What about a native cron UI in Hypertask? Not planned for now. Every workflow above is a few lines of config away, and the external-scheduler approach gives you logs, retries, alerts, and secret management for free. If you have a use case the external pattern does not cover, open an issue on the GitHub repo so we can see the gap. ## Scheduling orientation: Agents and next-task queue In addition to general-purpose agent workflows, you can configure agents to pull from a priority-scored next-task queue and act on their assigned tickets. The priority score reflects task urgency and value, and the queue exposes only claimable rows to prevent conflicts. To schedule a dedicated next-task queue agent: - Set up an external scheduler (GitHub Actions, cron, Cloudflare Worker, Vercel cron, etc.). - Have the scheduler disable the agentâ\x80\x99s ability to create unlimited tasks, and instead provide only a single-purpose command or endpoint for conditional next-task pulls (examples using the `hypertask` CLI or MCP are included in the other workflow patterns above). - On each run, the scheduler invokes an endpoint that: - Pulls ranked candidate tasks from the next-task queue for this board, - Checks that tasks are claimable by this agent (not already assigned), - If one or more candidate tasks are available, the scheduler creates a conditional task or comment for the agent: - With a conditional, the agent can pick up and claim one task from the queue on demand (default is the highest-priority available). - In the MCP or CLI flow, wrap the queue endpoint call to honor the schedulerâ\x80\x99s condition. Use a Context (via `hypertask_user_context` (`action: "get"`)) or an explicit owner ID to ensure the agent is authorized to claim the returned tasks. Treat the queue response as authoritative; update or close the created/conditional task as soon as the agent completes the work. **Recommended pattern on the MCP side** On every scheduled run, the scheduler calls a tool like `hypertask_tasks` with `action: "next"` and filtering options that ensure the results are claimable by this agent, then applies the schedulerâ\x80\x99s schema (e.g., `agent_id` or `team_id`). If the tool returns candidates, the routine for that agent creates a temporary task or comment to indicate it is ready to claim before it gets claimed; if the tool returns empty, the scheduler can sleep and retry on the next interval. When using code: - From the scheduler: call the endpoint; from an agent context: invoke the MCP tool. - After picking a task, the subsequent workflow should mark it as claimed (assign the agent owner) and transition the task to its normal workflow section; once the agent finishes, it can update the task, close the conditional slot, or delete the task as appropriate, then return to the queue endpoint for the next candidate. Example CLI flow (from a scheduler): ```bash #!/bin/bash # /home/you/hypertask-cron/next-task-handler.sh # Inspect the highest-priority unleased tasks without changing assignments. hypertask task next --project 15 # Claim the selected ticket in a separate agent step. hypertask agent take ``` This ensures: - Only tasks not already claimed are visible, - Priorities guide which tasks first, - The schedulerâ\x80\x99s condition gates behavior, - Agents run from an explicit, manageable queue. ---

title: AI Feedback from a Bot Account
description: Read reports and notifications from an AI Feedback bot account for events like failedlogin logins.
---


In Hypertask, events such as failed-login activity can be surfaced through an AI Feedback bot account. This account does not represent your personal identity; instead, it serves as a neutral feedback channel that system notifications can write to.

<Aside type="note">
System-level alerts are no longer written directly to your account. Instead, they use the dedicated bot so clear separation exists between user workflow and event logging.
</Aside>

### What is the AI Feedback bot account?

- **Account:** [ai-feedback@crolab.org](mailto:ai-feedback@crolab.org)
- **Purpose:** File reports like failed-login activity for visibility in the team workspace.
- **Identity:** The account is labeled "AI Feedback". Nothing associated with failed-login events is written as your personal account name.

### Use cases

- **Incident logging:** Failed-login attempts can be recorded as structured reports without exposing user identity.
- **Observability:** Team leads and administrators can monitor security-related events through the bot channel without sifting through individual inboxes.

### How it works

When the server logs failed-login activity, the event is written through the AI Feedback bot. For clarity, users who experience a failed login are not notified about how the report appears; only that the report exists in the workspace. This design keeps user workflows uninterrupted while preserving the event log.

System notifications about failed sign-in attempts are now filed via a dedicated bot account rather than a personal identity. Changes since claim:

--- title: Inbox & Notifications description: Manage your incoming notifications, Snooze, and Important section. --- The **Inbox** gathers all notifications (mentions, assignments, and more) into a single feed, letting you process them efficiently. Use keyboard shortcuts for quick actions and keep important work at the top of your queue. ## Viewing the inbox Press Ctrl + K to open the command palette and search for **"Inbox"**, or go to the Inbox page from the sidebar. The inbox shows: - **Unread notifications** from mentions, assignments, reactions, and follow updates - **Actionable items** like tasks, notifications with dismiss options (undo, dismiss all, undo all), and confirmed operations (invites, feedback) - **Important tasks**: rows marked with the **Important** label appear first, in priority order and timeline-sorted (newest first) ### Replying to notification emails Reply directly to a task notification email to add your response as a comment on the task. Send the reply from the same email address as your Hypertask account so Hypertask can verify it and post it under your name. The inbox can be grouped into multiple views:
Use Ctrl + F from the Inbox to search across all notifications. This is scoped across boards for board-agnostic filtering.
### Bulk archive Select multiple notifications with mouse clicks or keyboard navigation. When you select rows, the selection count appears next to the archive and remind icons, and the archive action archives all selected notifications in one step: | Action | Shortcut | Description | |--------|----------|-------------| | **Select all** | Ctrl + A | Select all visible rows in the current view, mirroring page behavior | | **Archive selected** | Shift + E | Archive all selected notifications | | **Archive all** | Ctrl + E | Archive all notifications (opens confirmation if many) |
Ctrl + A selects all visible rows rather than every row in the inbox due to index limits - select specific subsets when the list is long.
### Triage with AI chat Press Ctrl + K (Cmd + K on Mac). Choose **Triage inbox**. This starts a new AI chat. Ask AI chat to read your inbox. It reads up to 500 messages per page and can continue through the remaining pages without asking for confirmation. Before archiving a batch, chat previews every affected ticket, including other messages it would clear on those tickets. Confirm once for that batch. If the batch changes, chat shows a fresh preview and asks again. Its reply names the tickets it cleared. ### Inbox views | View | Shortcut | Purpose | |------|----------|---------| | **Inbox** | Default | All notifications | | **Search** | Search icon | Text-based search across all boards | | **Notifications** | Notification icon | List of all notification types | ### Inbox filtering scope New users in a board see notifications for private tasks, while users removed from a board no longer receive those notifications in their Inbox. To prevent a stale notification from reappearing, you can reply to it (or tap Undo) to remove it from your queue. Cleaning up unsubscribed notifications helps keep the Inbox focused and relevant. ## Agent chatter in the inbox Improvement Agent messages from the AI now stay out of the personal inbox. Agent-only comments (FYI messages) and agent chatter no longer appear as notifications for human users. Instead: - **Agent chatter ignored** – Pure agent commentary without a human @mention does not reach its owner's inbox. - **FYI mentions visible** – An agent FYI comment with a human @mention does appear in the inbox, making it clear the human is being included in the loop, but it stays out of the Important section. - **Only open questions land in Important** – When an agent poses a question that requires a human response, the message lands in the Important section so you can act on it first. This applies to all agents using Hypertask's AI integration and keeps your inbox focused on questions and actions directly tied to your own work. ## Numbered pins in the mobile inbox On mobile, each inbox row shows a numbered indicator next to the sender name. This creates a visual order that matches the date you received the notification, making it easier to scan recent items: - **Numbered pins** appear on desktop and mobile inbox rows - The numbers correspond to timeline order (newest first) - This keeps your attention on the most recent important items without relying solely on the top position
The numbered pins complement the timeline-sorted order for returning visits, giving you a quick visual guide to your recent notifications.
## Invite link validation across pages Improved Pages that generate or use invite links now validate board context. **My Tasks** and **Inbox** no longer send invite-link requests without a board, which previously caused console errors. Requesting an invite link without a board now shows a clear message instead of a server error, keeping the console clean and providing explicit feedback when a board is required. This change applies across most pages that send invite links, ensuring any invalid requests surface a user-friendly message rather than an unhandled error. ## Shortcuts tip visibility Improved When using the archive keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl + E or Shift + E), the tip that shows which shortcut to press (for example, "press E to archive") now appears and stays visible. The tip is tied to the bottom shortcut bar ("Ctrl+K for Command center, J to go down..."). Before this fix, repeatedly archiving would close the bottom shortcut bar or clear the inbox, causing the tip to disappear and making it hard to see which key shortcut to use. The tip is automatically disabled when the shortcut bar is hidden for the session, so navigating to the Inbox or re-opening the shortcut bar restores visibility. ## Board chip in the new task box When you use Ctrl+J to create a new task from the inbox, the new task box shows a board chip indicating the intended destination: - **Always visible**: The chip appears as soon as the box opens, so you always see the target board. - **Same everywhere**: On a board or a ticket detail page, it shows that page's board. - **Editable**: Click the chip to choose a different board before saving the task.
Ctrl+J uses the same board selection logic as the AI chat box: the focused ticket's board if there is one, otherwise the open board split, and finally the last used board for All or Important views.

title: Table View
description: Work with tasks in a responsive, adaptive Kanban-style table layout that matches Notion and Linear.
---


## Overview

Table view gives you a grid-based way to organize and manage tasks, similar to Notion or Linear. It adapts to the columns you need and keeps your layout preferences saved across sessions.

**Horizontal scrolling across all columns:** When a table's columns exceed the available width on your device (for example on narrow windows or very wide column sets), a visible horizontal scrollbar appears. This lets you scroll to see remaining columns in the grid without obscured headers or black space, ensuring you can reach every column in the row set.

**Unsaved sort states and saved views:** Sorting the table creates an unsaved view. An "orange Save view + Reset" indication appears in the header. Press Save to capture the sort configuration as a saved view, or Reset to discard it. Existing saved views reopen the table pre-sorted.

**Multiselect via Shift+E:** Press Shift+E to select the current row and add it to the selection set. From any multi-selected row, press Shift+E repeatedly to accumulate or extend the selection for bulk actions.

## Mouse-Accessible New Task Control

At the right end of a table's top row sits a quiet ghost button that creates new tasks. It provides a mouse-based way to add tasks without leaving the grid:

**Behavior:**
- With quick entry enabled, click **+ New task** to open a compact title field for the selected column.
- Press <kbd>Enter</kbd> to save each task and keep the empty field open for the next title. Press <kbd>Esc</kbd> to close it; reopening restores an unsaved title.
- Press <kbd>C</kbd> when you need the full task creator instead.
- Hidden from cross-board My Tasks tables.
- Uses only theme tokens so it matches your current customization.

**Accessibility:**
- Keyboard-focusable (tab into it, and Shift+Tab out).
- Excluded from the cross-board My Tasks table.
- Highlighted on hover and focus to make its purpose clear without taking up screen space.

## Adaptive layout

Table view automatically adjusts to the columns you're using:

- **Flexible title column:** The title column flexes to fill the remaining horizontal space; its width is a minimum, so you can use full width without nested scrolling or cramped visibility.
- **Flexible columns:** The table layout derives from your visible sections and columns, so you see the most relevant information without cramped spacing.
- **Full-title row behavior:** Press <kbd>Enter</kbd> to open a task focused on its description; the task detail view updates inline within the row, preserving the table layout without needing to leave the grid.

## Excel-style frozen panes

When you scroll horizontally across a table with many columns, the **Ticket** and **Title** columns stay visible while you view the rest of the grid. This frozen-pane behavior mimics Excel, ensuring the identifier and description of each row are always visible:

- **Ticket column**: Stays fixed on the far left, showing the task number consistently across scrolling
- **Title column**: Stays visible to the right of the Ticket column, keeping the task's primary label in view

This remains true for table layouts, board table views, and subtask tables, so you can always identify rows regardless of how far right you need to scroll.

## Column picker

Customize your table view with the column picker:

1. Press <kbd>Ctrl+K</kbd> and search for "Configure table" or "Column picker".
2. Select which columns to display and hide.
3. Click **APPLY** to persist your selection across sessions.

The palette in table view is the same one you get on the board, so board commands such as sorting, filter match mode, and board time tracking are all available without switching layouts.

Your column choices are saved per user, so each team member can have their own table layout.

<Aside type="tip">

The column picker and table layout are per-user settings. You can show or hide any column without deleting it, and changes apply immediately to your view.

</Aside>

## Move a task to another section

Drag any row onto another section's card and the task moves into that section. The row is the drag handle and the section card is the drop target, so nothing extra appears on screen; the card you are over takes the normal hover highlight.

Dragging is off in two cases, because a drop would be meaningless or wrong:

- **A column sort is active.** Rows render as one flat list with no section groups to drop into.
- **On /my-tasks.** Rows are grouped by due time or by board, not by a board column, so a move would target the wrong thing.

## The Created column

Turn on **Created** in the column picker to see when each task was opened, and click the header twice to sort oldest first.

It shows a real date rather than an age, because **On board** already gives you the age in days and "412d" does not tell you when something started. Dates outside the current year keep their year (`12 Sep, 2025`), so an old task can never be mistaken for a recent one. Sorting runs on the underlying timestamp, not the displayed text.

## Drag to reorder and resize

Drag columns directly to reorder them in place; the order stays in sync with the Table columns picker dropdown. Drag the column edge to resize each column to your preferred width. The title column remains locked as the leftmost column, with ticket detail keyed by title; the title column still flexes to fill leftover width.

### AMOLED hover and drag

On AMOLED displays, table resize handles are more visible:

- **Hover:** a 2px purple accent line appears on the edge while hovering over a column boundary.
- **Drag:** the guide line extends the full height of the table to show the planned column width.
- **Header feedback:** hovering any column header shows faint separators between columns for better discoverability of the grid.

### Excel-style resize model

Table view resize now follows an Excel-like model that gives you predictable control over column sizes:

- **First resize:** On your first resize of any column, the Title column's flex width is frozen at its rendered pixel width, making it fixed thereafter. All other columns reset to auto-fit width and wait for your next resize action.
- **Subsequent resizes:** After the initial resize, dragging any column edge follows your cursor 1:1 as you expand or shrink the column.
- **Wider grab strip:** Resize handles include a 12px wide grab strip that makes one-touch sizing easier on touch devices or small windows.
- **Reset to default:** Use the Table columns picker (e.g., ...) and click **Reset to default** (or Reset to original) to restore the original auto-fit width for all columns.

This Excel-style resize behavior ensures clearer feedback and deliberate resizing flow, especially when setting up a stable table layout.

## Advanced column configuration

Open the Configure table modal for more control over your table setup:

1. Press <kbd>Ctrl+K</kbd> and search for "Configure table".
2. In the column picker, click the ⋮ or **edit** icon next to "Columns" to open advanced options.
3. Choose from additional columns:

**Visibility options**
- **Visible columns** — toggle columns on and off without permanently deleting them. The table updates instantly.

**Additional columns**
- **Tags** — render label pills from your tags/column. Shows up to 3 pills, with "+N" expanding the rest. Pill clicks jump to other tasks with the same tag.
- **Comments** — count of comments per task with hover preview (up to 3 lines). Click to open the task.
- **Created** — full timestamp of task creation (e.g., "Jul 26, 2026 at 10:42 AM"). Click to view original creation.
- **Column** — which board section or column a task belongs to. Click to jump to that section on the board.
- **Status** — copy of the board column name for card-based views (e.g., "Done", "In Progress", "Review").
- **Stale** — indicator of task staleness when the board staleness toggle is enabled. Shows up to 7 days amber/red signal, empty when fresh, and hidden when the toggle is off. Click to sort by staleness (sorting column appears between Due and Updated).

**Actions**
- Drag columns by their grip handle to reorder them.
- Drag a column edge to resize to your preferred width.
- Click **Reset to default** or **Reset to original** to restore the original auto-fit layout.

<Aside type="note">

"Reset to default" or "Reset to original" places the Status column immediately after Title and moves Updated header to the right.

</Aside>

### Sort-Driven Columns

While sorting, the View engine adds columns to improve clarity:

- **Status column:** Appears immediately after Title, matching the board column name (e.g., Done, In Progress, Review). It hides when the sort is cleared.
- **Stale column (optional):** Only appears in the headers when sorting by staleness and the board staleness toggle is on. It hides again when staleness sorting is cleared or the toggle is off.

These additions keep the table focused around the sorted criteria without overwhelming you with every board field.

## Keyboard shortcuts

| Shortcut | Action |
|----------|--------|
| <kbd>Ctrl+K</kbd> | Open the command palette. Table view has the full board palette, including the column picker |
| <kbd>Shift+F</kbd> | Toggle focused search on the board |
| <kbd>W</kbd> | Start or stop the timer for the selected task |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> | Open task focused on description and keep the table layout |
| <kbd>Shift+E</kbd> | Select (or extend selection of) the current table row for bulk actions |

## Sorting behavior

When you sort a table, the experience tightens to show you the most useful columns at once:

- **Status column auto-shows** — as soon as you sort, a Status column appears immediately after the Title column, matching the board column name (e.g., Done, AI Review, Bugs). The column hides again when you clear the sort.
- **Updated header right-aligned** — the Updated header stays visibly right-aligned over the rest of the column headers.
- **Stale column option** — when sorting by staleness, a Stale column appears between Due and Updated headers. It hides when staleness sorting is cleared or when the board staleness toggle is off.

This pattern keeps the table focused on the sorted criteria without overwhelming you with every board field.

## Use cases

Table view is great for:

- **Analyzing lots of tasks:** See many items at once in a compact grid without losing readability.
- **Comparing priorities:** Side-by-side visibility of priority, size, and due dates.
- **Quick filtering:** Combine visibility filters with your column choices to surface the exact set of tasks you need.
- **Tracking staleness:** Use the Stale column to identify tasks that haven't been updated recently, especially on boards with staleness detection enabled.
- **Bulk work:** Combine multiselect with bulk actions (e.g., Move, Archive) for rapid processing.

## Scroll positions

**Full-height scroll container:** The scroll container reaches the bottom of the window, so the horizontal scrollbar stays pinned at the bottom regardless of row count. This ensures stable navigation when working with rows of any size.

title: Security and privacy
description: Sign-in methods, session length, account deletion, and where to read the privacy policy.
---

## Do you support SSO or SAML login?

No. Hypertask does not offer SSO, SAML, or SCIM.

You can sign in with Google, with email, or with a passkey. Email sign-in sends a temporary login link and a verification code. The login page shows **Sign in with a passkey** when the browser supports passkeys. Add or remove a passkey in **Settings → Profile → Accounts**.

A signed-in session lasts 30 days. Using Hypertask refreshes that session about once a day, which starts the 30 days again.

## Is Hypertask GDPR compliant, and where is my data stored?

The [privacy policy](https://hypertask.ai/privacy) is from Hypertask Lab Ltd. in London. It describes your right to request access to the personal information Hypertask holds, and to ask for a correction when that information is inaccurate, incomplete, or out of date. Third parties named in the policy include Google Analytics, Gmail, and Stripe. Google Calendar is included only if you connect it.

These docs do not state a data hosting region, and they do not include a data processing agreement. For data-processing questions, [contact support](https://docs.hypertask.ai/getting-started/contact-support/).

## Can I delete my account?

Yes. Open **Settings → Profile → General**. Under **Danger zone**, choose **Delete account**.

The screen says this wipes your boards and data, and that your email can sign up again from scratch. Confirming shows that this cannot be undone and that everything you own is wiped. Hypertask then signs you out.

Cancel your subscription before you delete the account. If a subscription is still active, deletion is refused, and the screen says it could not delete your account.

## Can I export my data?

There is no data export in the app. You can read tasks with the [REST API](/api/rest-api/) and the [CLI](/cli/reference/) (`hypertask task list`).

--- title: Agent webhooks description: Understand what wakes an agent, what Hypertask sends, how to verify it, and how to work without a public URL. --- A webhook is an instant notification from Hypertask to your agent. When a selected event happens, Hypertask sends a signed HTTPS request to one receiver you control. Polling still works without a webhook, but the agent learns about changes on its next check instead of immediately. ## Get your first verified delivery 1. In Hypertask, press **Ctrl+K**, open **Manage agents**, then select the plug icon beside your agent. 2. Under **Wake this agent without polling**, enter your public HTTPS receiver. Optionally limit delivery to one board or a subset of events. 3. Select **Save webhook** and store the signing secret. Hypertask shows it once. 4. Select **Send test**. Your receiver gets a real signed `webhook.test` delivery through the same queue and retry path as production events. 5. Confirm a 2xx result under **Recent deliveries**. Failed deliveries show their status and can be replayed.
Store the `whsec_…` signing secret in your secret manager. Hypertask masks it after creation. Rotate it if it is lost or exposed.
## Subscribe from an agent An agent bearer token manages its own endpoint with `self`. A human account token can replace `self` with an owned agent UUID. ```bash # Configure all addressed events hypertask webhook configure \ --url https://agent.example.com/hypertask \ --event comment.mention \ --event task.assigned \ --event task.unassigned \ --event comment.created \ --event task.updated \ --event task.created # Prove the receiver, signature, queue, and response path hypertask webhook test # Inspect delivery status hypertask webhook get ``` Use `--agent AGENT_UUID` when running with a human account token. Other commands are `replay DELIVERY_ID`, `rotate-secret`, and `delete`. Call `hypertask_webhooks` (`action: "configure"`): ```json { "action": "configure", "input": { "agent_id": "self", "url": "https://agent.example.com/hypertask", "events": ["comment.mention", "task.assigned", "task.unassigned", "comment.created", "task.updated", "task.created"] } } ``` Actions are `get`, `configure`, `test`, `replay`, `rotate`, and `delete`. `replay` also requires `delivery_id`. In private AI Chat, ask in plain language: > Configure the webhook for my Release Agent at https://agent.example.com/hypertask, then send a test. Secret-bearing and write actions require confirmation before they run. Hypertask shows a preview first; approve it in your next message. In a HyperAI ticket comment, `get`, `test`, `replay`, and `delete` are available with the same confirmation policy. Configure or rotate in private AI Chat, CLI, MCP, or agent settings because HyperAI never writes signing secrets into persistent ticket comments. ```bash curl -X POST https://app.hypertask.ai/api/mcp/webhooks \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $AGENT_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "action": "configure", "agent_id": "self", "url": "https://agent.example.com/hypertask", "events": ["comment.mention", "task.assigned", "task.unassigned", "comment.created", "task.updated", "task.created"] }' ``` The response contains `secret` once. Read configuration and recent attempts with: ```bash curl "https://app.hypertask.ai/api/mcp/webhooks?agent_id=self" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $AGENT_TOKEN" ``` ## Board-level webhooks Each managed agent has one webhook subscription. Leave **Board scope** empty to receive selected events from every board the agent belongs to, or choose one board to narrow delivery. Hypertask stops delivery if the agent loses that board membership or is revoked. Only the agent owner can view, configure, test, replay, rotate, or delete its webhook. Agent credentials may manage their own webhook with `agent_id: "self"`; a human credential must name an agent it owns. ## Verify the signature Hypertask signs the exact raw request bytes. Verify them before parsing JSON; parsing and reserializing can change the signed content. | Header | Meaning | |---|---| | `X-Hypertask-Event` | Event name, including `webhook.test` | | `X-Hypertask-Timestamp` | Unix time used in the signature | | `X-Hypertask-Delivery` | Stable ID used to deduplicate automatic retries | | `X-Hypertask-Signature` | `sha256=` followed by the lowercase HMAC hex digest | ```text signed content = X-Hypertask-Timestamp + "." + raw request bytes signature = "sha256=" + HMAC-SHA256(signing secret, signed content) ``` Use a constant-time comparison and reject timestamps outside your replay window. The examples use five minutes. ```js const app = express(); const secret = process.env.HYPERTASK_WEBHOOK_SECRET; app.post("/hypertask", express.raw({ type: "application/json" }), (req, res) => { const rawBody = req.body; const timestamp = req.header("x-hypertask-timestamp") ?? ""; const received = req.header("x-hypertask-signature") ?? ""; const timestampSeconds = Number(timestamp); if (!secret || !Buffer.isBuffer(rawBody) || !Number.isFinite(timestampSeconds) || Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - timestampSeconds) > 300) { return res.sendStatus(401); } const digest = createHmac("sha256", secret) .update(`${timestamp}.`) .update(rawBody) .digest("hex"); const expected = `sha256=${digest}`; const left = Buffer.from(received, "utf8"); const right = Buffer.from(expected, "utf8"); if (left.length !== right.length || !timingSafeEqual(left, right)) { return res.sendStatus(401); } const deliveryId = req.header("x-hypertask-delivery"); const payload = JSON.parse(rawBody.toString("utf8")); res.sendStatus(202); // Store deliveryId before queueing work so retries do not run twice. }); ``` ```python from flask import Flask, request app = Flask(__name__) secret = os.environ["HYPERTASK_WEBHOOK_SECRET"].encode() @app.post("/hypertask") def handle_webhook(): raw_body = request.get_data(cache=True) timestamp = request.headers.get("X-Hypertask-Timestamp", "") received = request.headers.get("X-Hypertask-Signature", "") try: if abs(time.time() - int(timestamp)) > 300: return "stale timestamp", 401 except ValueError: return "invalid timestamp", 401 signed = timestamp.encode() + b"." + raw_body expected = "sha256=" + hmac.new(secret, signed, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest() if not hmac.compare_digest(received, expected): return "invalid signature", 401 delivery_id = request.headers.get("X-Hypertask-Delivery") payload = json.loads(raw_body) # queueAgentWork(delivery_id, payload) return "", 202 ``` ## Events and payloads | Event | When it fires | Event-only fields | |---|---|---| | `comment.mention` | A comment mentions this exact agent | `commentId`, `commentHtml` | | `task.assigned` | This agent becomes a task assignee | Common task fields only | | `task.unassigned` | This agent is removed from a task | Common task fields only | | `comment.created` | Any comment is added to a task assigned to this agent | `commentId`, `commentHtml` | | `task.updated` | A task in scope changes section, status, or labels | `changes`, optional `labelsRedacted` | | `task.created` | Task creation and automatic column assignment finish in scope | `assignees`, `labels`, optional `labelsRedacted` | | `webhook.test` | The owner selects **Send test** or requests a test | `test: true`, `message`; no task fields | Task event payloads include `event`, `deliveryId`, `occurredAt`, `agentId`, `projectId`, `taskId`, nullable `ticketNumber`, `taskTitle`, and `actor`. Event-only fields appear as shown above. A test payload has the common delivery fields but no task or actor. ```json { "event": "comment.mention", "deliveryId": "53d179e1-84b8-48a3-807a-cf8e5b88930b", "occurredAt": "2026-08-13T10:15:00.000Z", "agentId": "f95165ad-36b3-4d87-af70-547df78e17c1", "projectId": 15, "taskId": 27397, "taskTitle": "Outbound webhooks for agent mentions and assignments", "commentId": 182293, "commentHtml": "

@Release Agent please review

", "actor": { "userId": 6, "agentId": null, "displayName": "Valentin Yeo" } } ``` ## Test and replay **Send test** creates a real `webhook.test` delivery for the active subscription. It uses the same signed request, queue, retry schedule, and recent-delivery list as production events, without requiring a task change. **Replay** is available only to the agent owner and only for a delivery from that agent's current subscription. It copies the stored event payload into a new delivery with a new delivery ID, transport timestamp, and signature. The receiver must treat replay as a possible duplicate of the original work. ## Delivery behavior - Hypertask sends the first `POST` immediately with `Content-Type: application/json`. - Return any 2xx response within **5 seconds**. Queue longer work after responding. - A failed `chat.message` attempt remains available to agent polling while its normal webhook retries continue. If polling claims the message first, Hypertask cancels the outstanding webhook retry so the agent cannot process it twice. Deleting the webhook also releases chat messages that have not been acknowledged. - Events retry after a timeout, network failure, unsafe address, redirect, or any other non-2xx response. Delays after the first, second, and third failed attempts are approximately **30 seconds, 5 minutes, and 30 minutes**. Delivery stops after four total attempts. - Automatic retries keep the exact body and delivery ID. Each attempt gets a fresh timestamp and signature. Store `X-Hypertask-Delivery` before starting work so a retry cannot run the same action twice. - Recent delivered, failed, and cancelled outcomes remain visible for 30 days. ## No public HTTPS URL A webhook cannot point to `localhost` or a private network address. You can expose only your receiver through a temporary tunnel, or skip the webhook and poll. ### Use a temporary Cloudflare Tunnel 1. Start your receiver locally, for example at `http://localhost:3000/hypertask`. 2. Run `cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:3000`. 3. Copy the generated `https://…trycloudflare.com` address, add `/hypertask`, and save it as the webhook endpoint. 4. Select **Send test**, then confirm a 2xx result under **Recent deliveries**.
Expose only the webhook route. Do not run a debug server or expose admin routes. Keep the signing secret in an environment variable, do not print secrets or full production payloads, and stop the tunnel when testing ends. Quick Tunnel addresses change when restarted, so update the saved endpoint before testing again.
### Poll instead A webhook is optional. `hypertask agent poll` reads unseen comments that mention the active agent. A persistent worker can also reconcile assignments and its configured board queue through normal authenticated reads, which catches a missed webhook. ```bash hypertask agent poll \ --project "$PROJECT_ID" \ --agent-id "$AGENT_ID" \ --agent-name "$AGENT_NAME" ``` Polling cadence belongs to the worker deployment, not the Hypertask API. Set an explicit active and idle interval in the worker profile. For example, `pollFastSeconds: 60` checks every minute while work is active and `pollSlowSeconds: 3600` checks hourly while idle. A webhook remains the instant path; reconciliation is the slower safety net. ## Troubleshooting | Symptom | Check | |---|---| | No secret appears | Secrets are shown only after first configuration or rotation. Rotate if the original was not stored. | | Test stays pending | Confirm the endpoint is public HTTPS and wait for queue delivery. If it is local, start the tunnel and save its current address. | | `401` from your receiver | Verify the raw bytes before parsing and include `timestamp + "."` before the body. | | Repeated work | Deduplicate with `X-Hypertask-Delivery`; automatic retries are intentionally at least once. | | `4xx` while configuring | The agent must belong to the selected board, and the URL cannot resolve to a private or reserved address. | | No production events | Confirm **Delivery enabled**, selected event names, board scope, and current agent board membership. |

## `hypertask chat listen`

```text
Poll the agent inbox, send a fresh heartbeat, and print each new message once across restarts. Run hypertask chat listen in the background; answer with hypertask chat reply <chat-id> --text <text>. Usage: hypertask chat listen [options]

Options:
  --once
      Send one heartbeat and poll once, then exit (nonzero on error).
  --interval <s>
      Polling interval in whole seconds (1-60, default 5); errors back off exponentially up to 60 seconds.

Example:
  hypertask chat listen --once

  -h, --help

```

## `hypertask login`

```text
Login to HyperTask via browser

Usage: hypertask login [options]

Options:
  --token <jwt>
      JWT token (skip browser auth)
  --code <code>
      Five-minute agent sign-in code
  --api-url <url>
      API URL

Example:
  hypertask login --token <jwt>

      Show help
```

### Guided start after token login

```bash
hypertask login --token <token> --human
```

```text
Signed in as Claude Code (agent of Maria Lopez)
Board: Product Launch
https://app.hypertask.ai/project?id=9142

Next steps your agent can run now:
  1. See the board:          hypertask task list --project 9142
  2. Create a first task:    hypertask task create --project 9142 --title "My first task"
  3. Read the board rules:   hypertask project playbook 9142

Or just ask your agent: "What's on my Hypertask board?"
```

Token login checks the token right away. On success, it shows who you are signed in as and the newest board across all boards the token can see. A missing title falls back to the short name. The example above uses a fictional write agent and board.

The CLI prints the server's steps: read-only agents get two steps, list and playbook, with no create step. If no board is available, `--human` says "No board yet. Create one in your Hypertask web app."

JSON is the default output. It keeps `success`, `saved`, and `configPath`, and adds:

| Field | What it contains |
|-------|------------------|
| `signedInAs` | The signed-in identity, including `name`. |
| `board` | The board's `id`, `title`, and `url`. |
| `nextSteps` | The server's suggested steps (three for write agents, two for read-only agents, none without a board), each with a CLI `command`. |
| `moreBoards` | A hint to run `hypertask project list` when the token can see several boards. |

The CLI waits at most about 1.5 seconds for the guide. If it times out or fails because of a network or server error, login still saves the token. It returns the previous saved-token output without the guided start. Saving a token does not mean the check passed.

title: Calendar
description: Day, week, and month views, keyboard navigation, and shareable calendar links.
---


The calendar at `/calendar` shows every task with a due date across your boards. Filter which boards and people are included from the boards panel, and save any combination as a reusable view.

<Aside type="tip">

You can enshrine your preferred weekday start and weekend visibility by saving a preset, or rely on the default behavior for a fresh calendar.

</Aside>

## Default behavior

When you open a calendar without a saved preference:

- **Week starts on Monday** (Day and Week views show Monday through Friday; weekends are not shown). If you prefer Sunday as the starting day or want to show weekend rows, change your preference in Settings.
- **Weekend days are hidden in Week view** (you still see Monday through Friday). If you prefer to see the full week including Saturday and Sunday, adjust your preference in Settings.

To change your default weekday start or weekend visibility, go to Settings and set your preferred options. Controls are surfaced via <kbd>Ctrl+K</kbd> commands (if configured).

## Managing calendar views

Default views include Day, Week, Month, My Tasks, Overdue, Blocked, and Agents. All default views are ordinary orderable views: you can drag them anywhere in the view cluster, including up to an earlier row. You can also show each default view in Manage views (drag + hide) and reorder it alongside saved custom views.

From **Manage calendar views**, you can rename any calendar view that you own. Owned views show a settings affordance that lets you edit the name. Teammate-owned views are locked and cannot be renamed. The modal includes a clear close/back control for safe, deliberate switching between saved and owned views.

## Views

Switch views from the dropdown at the top left (or press <kbd>W</kbd> for week, <kbd>M</kbd> for month):

- **Day**: full-width table layout with tasks as rows. Use <kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>D</kbd> to switch to day view. On desktop, Day view now includes a weekday-selector strip above the calendar. To jump to a specific weekday, click any weekday label in the strip. Keyboards actions <kbd>U</kbd> and <kbd>I</kbd> move to previous/next day; <kbd>T</kbd> jumps to today; <kbd>Tab</kbd> and <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>Tab</kbd> move focus; <kbd>Shift</kbd>+arrows reschedule the focused task.
- **Week**: five columns with hidden weekends (by default), or seven columns if you show weekends.
- **Month**: the classic grid.

## Shareable links

The calendar URL always encodes what you are looking at:

```
https://app.hypertask.ai/calendar?view=day&date=2026-07-31
```

- `view` is `day`, `week`, or `month`.
- `date` is the anchor day in `YYYY-MM-DD`.

Copy a link at any time to share exactly the same view and date. Open a shared link to land on that day's specific view, regardless of the recipient's own last-used calendar state. Links with invalid dates fall back to the recipient's own calendar.

For agents: construct these URLs directly when pointing a person at a specific day or week, e.g. `https://app.hypertask.ai/calendar?view=week&date=2026-08-03`.

## Week strip month expander

In the Week view, a month expander lets you quickly jump to any month. When you change days or weeks using arrows or navigation controls, the picker now stays in sync with your current view instead of remembering the month it opened with.

## Rendering reliability

The calendar renders reliably in production even when a persisted user state is null. Server-side identity-dependent calendar filters use the validated account ID passed from the server boundary, preventing SSR crashes on boards with missing user configurations.

## Legacy image support

If your board has historical images stored with an old S3 host configuration, the calendar no longer crashes when loading those images. Hypertask now accepts legacy bucket hosts in `next.config` remotePatterns, so old images load without bringing down the entire page. Requesting an official image migration, which will rewrite stored URLs to `files.hypertask.app`, remains a separate data cleanup effort. The calendar now works smoothly even when some images are still on an old host.

## Blocked tasks

Blocked tasks now stand out in Calendar. Month, week, and day views show the same red left edge as the board, making it easy to spot bottlenecks at a glance without switching to your board view.

On mobile agenda cards, blocked tasks now show the person blocking them with a red chip. This chip appears on both blocked and unblocked calendar agenda rows, so you can always see who's holding up work at a glance.

The CLI help and capabilities tools also require login now, and login prompts explain where to obtain a token when one isn't available. ### Tasks [HTPR-7121](https://app.hypertask.ai/detail/project-15/7121) - Fixed vague "Resource not found" errors when an agent creates a ticket with a wrong column or label. The server now provides clear, actionable messages: "Section with ID {id} not found in project {projectId}" and "Label with name '{name}' not found in project {projectId}. Labels given by name work correctly." ### Flags [HTPR-7084](https://app.hypertask.ai/detail/project-15/7084) - Fixed the Flags page to show every flag's real type (Bug, Feature, or Improvement) instead of always showing "Bug". title: Agents Dashboard
description: View all your agents from a central dashboard, with detail pages for each agent, board-scoped view, and status toggles at a glance.
---


# Agents Dashboard

The **Agents Dashboard** gives you a central view of your agents, including summary statistics, per-agent details, and board-scoped dashboards.

## Access the Agents Dashboard

- **URL**: `https://app.hypertask.ai/agents`
- From any page, use `Cmd+K` (Mac), `Ctrl+K` (Windows/Linux) and search for **"Go to Agents"**.

## Agent list by status

The overview page (`/agents`) groups your agents into three top-level sections:

- **Running** — agents currently active and executing tasks.
- **Quiet** — agents not currently running, but ready to start.
- **Off** — agents paused or stopped.

Each group displays agent cards showing key information.

## Agent cards

Each agent card shows:

- **Agent name** — the agent identifier.
- **Status** — Running, Quiet, or Off.
- **On/Off toggle** — pause or resume the agent.
- **Heartbeat line** for the merge/unblock timer.
- **Avatar** — a generated robot icon for each agent.

### Heartbeat line

The heartbeat line visualizes the agent's 10-minute merge/unblock check:

- **Green dot, short bar** — timer ran within the last 15 minutes.
- **Amber dot, medium bar** — timer ran between 15–30 minutes ago.
- **Red dot, no bar** — timer missed its 10-minute window or no data available.

### Card outlines

A red outline signals a **blocked** agent — no one is actively working on it. This helps you spot bottlenecks at a glance.

### Blocked-summary widget

A blocked-summary widget shows the number of agents currently blocked, helping you prioritize follow-up work.

## Board-scoped agent pages

Each board has its own dedicated agent page showing the agents configured for that board:

- **URL format**: `https://app.hypertask.ai/agents/<board-number>`
- Example: Board 5500 is available at `https://app.hypertask.ai/agents/5500`.

The board page includes:

- Board-specific agent list.
- Toolkit bug totals, including AGTE tickets tagged as bug.
- Configuration source: board, repository, branch, and agent list read from a shared setup.
- Main merge counts or reference links for the board.

Use board pages to inspect board-level agent health and bug tracking per board.

## Per-agent availability

All agents show generated robot avatars from their detail pages and the dashboard. This provides visual recognition without relying on initials or external icons.

### Agent examples

| Agent | Status |
|---|---|
| Preview Bot | Running |
| QA Agent | Quiet |
| Scheduler | Off |

## Performance and reliability

Use the agents page to:

- Spot which agents are actively working.
- Pause or resume agents consuming resources.
- Monitor agent distribution across workflows.
- Identify blocked agents via red outlines and the blocked-summary widget.

## MCP client evaluation frame

When the MCP client eval is enabled, the agents page displays a table of 20 real Hypertask tasks run through the MCP server and CLI. Each row shows pass/fail, token in/out, wall time, and tool call count. This helps you compare MCP to the CLI and catch regressions.

## Working with pages and task detail pages

Agents can reference task detail pages (e.g., `/detail/project-15/<ticket>`) via the production verifier, enabling them to verify lifecycles and create links as part of workflows.

## Troubleshooting

<Aside type="note">

If you don't see an agent in the dashboard, check that:

1. The agent is connected to an active board.
2. The agent schedule has necessary permissions.
3. The agent is associated with your team or scope.

See [AI Agents](/features/agents/) and [Scheduling Agents](/mcp/scheduling/) for setup details.

</Aside>
