--- title: CLI Reference description: Complete reference for the Hypertask CLI to manage tasks, projects, comments, and notifications from your terminal. --- The native Hypertask CLI lets you manage tasks, projects, comments, and notifications from your terminal. The executable is named `hypertask`. The CLI ships as a native Zig binary (htz) and can also be installed via npm. Connecting an agent token? See [Connect a new agent](/connect-an-agent/). ## Find blockers ```bash hypertask blockers --user me hypertask blockers --user 123 --project 15 --project 42 --state waiting --json hypertask inbox list --waiting-on me ``` `blockers` lists tasks waiting on the chosen person across accessible boards. Use `me` or a numeric user ID with `--user`. Repeat `--project` to limit the results to specific board IDs, and add `--json` for JSON output. `hypertask inbox list --waiting-on me` is an alias. Each result includes the marked question, recommendation, task link, board and column, priority, and wait time. Filter with `--state`: - `waiting`: no human reply or reaction after the question. - `answered`: the chosen person replied after the question or reacted to it. - `no-question`: the task has no marked Question. These commands are read-only; they do not clear blockers. ## Install ### Via npm (recommended) ```bash npm install -g @hypertask/hypertask_cli@latest ``` This installs a lightweight npm shim that fetches and runs the official htz binary for your platform, ensuring you always have the latest version. ### Via curl (Linux / macOS) On Linux or macOS, run: ```bash curl -fsSL https://hypertask.ai/install | sh hypertask --version ``` The installer detects x64 or ARM64, downloads the matching binary from the latest [GitHub release](https://github.com/hypertask-ai/cli/releases), and verifies its SHA-256 checksum. It installs to `~/.local/bin` by default. Set `HYPERTASK_INSTALL_DIR` to choose another directory. ### Via PowerShell (Windows x64) On Windows x64, run in PowerShell: ```powershell irm https://hypertask.ai/install.ps1 | iex hypertask --version ``` The installer downloads the native executable from the latest [GitHub release](https://github.com/hypertask-ai/cli/releases), verifies its SHA-256 checksum, installs it to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Hypertask` and adds that folder to your user `PATH`. Open a new terminal afterwards to run `hypertask` from anywhere. Set `HYPERTASK_INSTALL_DIR` to choose another directory. ### Fleet auto-install behavior When you merge a commit into the hypertask-ai/cli repository, the VPS fleet runs an automated install workflow: - The trusted runner builds the htz binary in ReleaseFast mode. - It preserves any existing symlinks under `~/.local/bin`. - It only considers the install successful after verifying the installed binary matches the freshly built commit. - Previous verifications and log metadata are retained to detect drift or mismatches. If an install does not succeed, the CI/CD pipeline fails and prevents the commit from being considered merged. ## Inside the Hypertask App When you choose to install Hypertask from the web app, the in-app installer (CLI install dialog) uses the npm shim to fetch the htz binary for you. This keeps the command identical across all install channels. ## General behaviour ### Unknown flags The CLI fails out loud for unrecognized flags and options. An unknown flag results in an error message and an exit code of 2 (non-zero), indicating a configuration or usage error. ```bash hypertask task get HYFA-70 --zzznotaflag 9 # unknown option: --zzznotaflag # exit code: 2 ``` ### Ticket commands `hypertask ticket` is the same command as `hypertask task`, so `hypertask ticket get HTPR-8265`, `hypertask ticket list --project 15` and `hypertask help ticket get` do exactly what their `task` forms do. Your brief and the board call them tickets, and the CLI answers both words instead of rejecting `ticket` as an unknown command. ### Reading a ticket by number A bare number is an internal task id, so it can belong to any board. `hypertask task get 8263` names the ticket and board it did read, and when no task has that id it names the two shapes that reach the ticket: the ticket key, or `--project` with the board. ```bash hypertask task get 8263 # no task has id 8263. A bare number is a task id on any board; pass the ticket key, or --project with the board, when it is a ticket number hypertask task get 8263 --project 15 hypertask task get HTPR-8263 ``` ### Reading a ticket from its app link A ticket link copied from the address bar works wherever the CLI takes a ticket. The board and the ticket number are read from the link, so a pasted link does what `8263 --project 15` does. A `#comment-` anchor, a query string and later path segments are ignored, and a `--project` that names another board is refused instead of reading the wrong one. ```bash hypertask task get https://app.hypertask.ai/detail/project-15/8456 hypertask comment list https://app.hypertask.ai/detail/project-15/8456 --limit 5 ``` ### Comment text from a file `comment add --file ` reads the comment text from a file, and that file holds HTML, the same as `--text`. Add `--markdown` when the file holds Markdown instead. ```bash hypertask comment add HTPR-2992 --file comment.html ``` `--html-file` is not a `comment add` flag; it belongs to `report create` and `report update`. A wrong flag is refused with exit code 2, and the error lists the flags that command does accept. ### Unknown commands A command that does not exist is answered as a command: `hypertask task lst HYFA-70 --project 15` prints `unknown command: lst`, the commands that do exist, and `did you mean: list`, instead of blaming the flag that followed it. When the guessed word lives under another command, the answer says where the work is. From v0.2.35, `hypertask task comments HYFA-70` answers `unknown command: comments` and `a ticket's comments are read with: hypertask comment list `. A board's columns are sections, and the answer says so. From v0.2.36, `hypertask board --help` and `hypertask board sections --project 15` both answer `board columns are sections: hypertask section list --project `. The same version accepts `column` and `columns` as names for `section`, so `hypertask columns list --project 15` reads the columns. ```bash hypertask columns list --project 15 # same output as: hypertask section list --project 15 ``` ### Agent log An agent's work notes belong in a ticket's agent log, not in comments for people. `hypertask activity` is the same command as `hypertask comment`, so `activity add` writes that log: the note is saved and nobody is notified. ```bash hypertask activity add HTPR-1 --text "Checked the deploy log; the build passed." # Saved to the agent log (no comment, nobody notified). ``` Post a comment for people with `--kind question`, `qa` or `done`. Read the log back with `hypertask task agent-log `, and `hypertask activity last ` answers where the log is read instead of listing the comment commands. From v0.2.38. ### Ticket identifiers A ticket has a short key, like `HTPR-8537`, and a list prints an internal `id` too. The two share one number range, so a bare number is the internal id, and that id can sit on any board. A read names the ticket it landed on: ```bash hypertask task get 1172 # 1172 is task id 1172: HTPR-481 on Hypertask. A bare number is an internal id on any board; # pass the ticket number, or --project with the board, when the board matters ``` A write cannot be undone, so a write that names a bare number writes nothing: ```bash hypertask activity add 1172 --text "note" # nothing was written: 1172 is task id 1172: HTPR-481 on Hypertask. # Pass the ticket number to write to the ticket, or id:1172 to write to that task # exit code: 2 ``` Write with the ticket key (`hypertask activity add HTPR-481 --text "note"`), a bare ticket number plus `--project `, or `id:` when you mean the internal id. This covers `comment add`, `activity add`, `task update`, `task assign`, `task unassign`, `task description restore` and `task inbox move`. ### Error reports From v0.2.18, when a command fails unexpectedly (a server error, a network problem, a response the CLI cannot read, or an internal error), the CLI sends Hypertask one short report so the failure becomes a bug ticket. The report holds only the command name (like `task create`), the error type, the HTTP status, the CLI version and your operating system. It never includes task content, ids, arguments or your token. Your own mistakes (an unknown flag, a missing task, no permission) are never reported. Reporting never changes the error message or exit code, and gives up after about 1.5 seconds. To turn it off, set `HYPERTASK_NO_ERROR_REPORTS=1`, or add `"error_reports": false` to `~/.hypertask/config.json`. ### v0.2.16 CLI Release (2026-10-12) This release fixes a crash when running AI reviews on large pull requests. The CLI now passes PR text to the review program through standard input instead of a command-line argument, preventing shell argument limits: - **No crash on large PRs:** AI review commands now work on arbitrarily large pull requests without hitting shell argument limits. - **Internal program path consistency:** The review program running on the server matches the code stored in the repository, verified in QA. To upgrade to v0.2.16: ```bash npm install -g @hypertask/hypertask_cli@latest hypertask --version ``` ### v0.2.15 CLI Release (2026-10-11) This release fixes a bug in agent emoji handling for CLI inbox operations. The CLI now correctly distinguishes between agent and human reactions: - Agent emoji reactions are no longer counted as human reactions in the CLI inbox. - Human reactions are no longer dropped when loading or processing inbox data. Previously, the CLI would treat an agent's emoji as if it came from a person, potentially causing selection or counting errors in inbox actions like bulk archive. This fix ensures accurate reaction tracking for agents monitoring tasks. To upgrade to v0.2.15: ```bash npm install -g @hypertask/hypertask_cli@latest hypertask --version ``` ### v0.2.19 CLI Release (2026-10-15) CLI 0.2.19 improves error reporting when network problems occur during command execution. - **Read retries and clearer errors:** If the server does not respond while the CLI waits, it now retries once and surfaces the actual error instead of a bare "ReadFailed" message. Use `--help` or the full command list (`hypertask capabilities --json`) to see available updates. This change applies to all commands that involve waiting for a server response, including task listing, task details, and other read operations. --- ## Task listing with label filters ### hypertask tasks list List tasks with optional filtering. ```bash hypertask tasks list [options] ``` **Options:** | Option | Description | |--------|-------------| | `--query ` | Free-text search. Same flag on every list command. | | `--filter ` | Repeatable structured filter. Keys: `priority`, `section`, `label`, `assignee`, `status`, `updated_since`, `has_pr`. | | `--sort ` | Sort, for example `updatedAt:desc`. | | `--fields ` | Return only these columns, for example `title,url`. | | `--labels ` | Filter tasks by one or more labels. | | `--limit ` | Max rows. | | `--cursor ` | Next page from the previous response. | | `--offset ` | Start listing from the Nth item (for paginated results). | **Behaviour:** - Returns a paginated list of tasks matching the specified filters. - Prefer `--query`, `--filter`, `--fields`, and `--limit` so one call stays small. - Use `--offset` or `--cursor` to walk large collections. ```bash hypertask tasks list --project 15 --filter section=AI Review --filter has_pr=red --fields title,url --limit 20 hypertask tasks list --labels cli,urgent ```
The `tasks list --labels` flag was previously a no-op. It now correctly filters tasks by the provided labels.
The `--filter priority` option now accepts both priority names (`urgent`, `high`, `medium`, `low`, `none`) and numeric values (0–4), matching the web UI and API. `none` matches tasks without an assigned priority.
## Task move ### hypertask tasks move Move a task from one section to another. This works within a board or across boards. ```bash hypertask tasks move --section hypertask tasks move --to hypertask tasks move --to --to-section ``` **Options:** | Option | Description | |--------|-------------| | `--section ` | Move the task to this section within the same board. | | `--to ` | Move the task to this board. Use `--to-section` to specify the target section in the new board. | | `--to-section ` | Specify the target section in the board given by `--to`. If omitted, the section defaults to "Backlog". | | `--assignee ` | Change the task's assignee instead of moving it. | **Behaviour:** - If the task is archived, the command fails with: > "Archived tasks cannot move sections or change assignees" - Use `--to ` to move a task to a different board, optionally with `--to-section` to specify a target section in the new board. - Use `--assignee ` to change the task's assignee without moving boards. ```bash # Move a task to another board (defaults to Backlog in the target board) hypertask tasks move INFRA-123 --to 15 # Move a task to another board and specific section hypertask tasks move INFRA-123 --to 15 --to-section 4060 # Move a task to a different section in the same board hypertask tasks move PRODUCT-456 --section "In Review" # Move a task and change its assignee hypertask tasks move PRODUCT-456 --assignee @valentin ```
The `comments add --improve` flag now correctly accepts a bare flag without a value and defaults to readability improvement.
## Project management errors are informative Bug fix Task creation now reports project membership failures with clear guidance instead of showing an internal server error or generic failure when the token lacks access. Previously, using a non-member token to create a task resulted in a generic "hypertask: the server could not complete the command" exit code 4. After this fix, the same command returns: ```bash # Using a token without project 5156 access hypertask task create --project 5156 --section Backlog # error: you are not a project member. Sign in with a valid account or use a token that has access to project 5156. # exit code: 4 ``` This makes CLI errors actionable for debugging out-of-scope work and bot configurations. --- ## Project management ### hypertask project update Update a project (board) by ID. To rename a board, use the `--title` flag: ```bash hypertask project update --title "" ``` **Options:** | Option | Description | |--------|-------------| | `--title ` | New board title. The title will be trimmed to non-empty and max 200 characters. | | `--description <description>` | Optional board description (HTML). | **Behaviour:** - Board members with write access can rename the board; non-members are blocked with a clear error. - Empty or overly long titles are rejected locally with a helpful message. - Only board members are allowed to update the board: an unknown board ID returns "not found", while a non-member receives "Not allowed to rename this board". ```bash # Rename a board by ID hypertask project update 4060 --title "Agents & Infra" # Update the description as well hypertask project update 4060 --title "Agents & Infra" --description "<p>Infrastructure-related tasks and boards.</p>" ``` <span class="label label--brand">Behavior change</span> Renaming a board from the app previously did not check board membership; agents and users could rename boards they were not members of. Board updates now require write access to the board. Only board members are allowed to update the board. --- You can also manage board columns and saved views with: - `hypertask view create` — Create a saved view. - `hypertask view list` — List saved views for a project. - `hypertask view switch <view-id>` — Switch to a saved view. For more options, run `hypertask project --help`, `hypertask view --help`, or `hypertask tasks --help`. Help names where a topic's help lives. `hypertask help project`, `hypertask project --help` and `hypertask --help project` all print that command's page, so a help request reaches any command, not only `features`. `hypertask help features` lists live product features, and `hypertask help` with no topic prints the top page, which ends with the list of commands. A topic that is not a command answers with where that help lives instead of `unknown command`. ## Delete a board from the CLI Only the board owner or a board admin can delete a board. Sign in to the CLI with an account or token that has that permission. <Aside type="caution"> Deletion removes the board and all its tasks. It cannot be undone through the CLI. Check the board ID before continuing. To keep the board for later, archive it instead. </Aside> First, check the board you want to delete: ```bash hypertask project show <board-id> ``` Then delete it with explicit confirmation: ```bash hypertask project delete <board-id> --yes ``` Replace `<board-id>` with the board's numeric ID. Without `--yes`, the CLI refuses to delete it. Ordinary board membership is not enough. The board must be active. If it is archived, ask its owner to restore it before deleting: ```bash hypertask project archive <board-id> --restore ``` For a reversible alternative, the board owner can archive it: ```bash hypertask project archive <board-id> ```

title: API-created tasks appear in search immediately
description: Tasks created via API or quick-add now show in search pipeline within seconds, without requiring a title edit to index.
---

API-created tasks now appear in search within seconds after creation, without requiring a title rename or edit to trigger indexing. Previously, tickets created through the API or quick-add on a board would not appear in search until their title was saved again.

**How it works:**

The POST /api/v1/tasks endpoint now initiates a search index update after each creation. On desktop and mobile, new tasks indexed via the API or quick-add are discoverable within a few seconds. Background indexing caches result payloads for publisher handles and subjects, reducing redo logic.

**Detected use cases:**

API-created tasks join search results alongside manual creation. Quick-add from boards and fullscreen new-task windows follow the same pattern. Reindexed tasks show title search results consistent with board/card structure and task-type tags.

**Evidence:**

Live test passed on 2026-10-11:
- Ticket made via API found in search after ~6 seconds.
- Quick-add from board found after ~3 seconds.
- Fullscreen new-ticket window found after ~3 seconds.

See [https://app.hypertask.ai/detail/project-15/7131](https://app.hypertask.ai/detail/project-15/7131)

title: Billing & Seat Management
description: Add and manage seat licenses, view cost forecasts, and test billing flows safely.
---


Hypertask billing controls license capacity, seat limits, and access tiers. Manage seats, track costs, and safely test billing changes in production without risking database side effects.

## Your billing label in Stripe

Stripe uses your team name as the display name on invoices and in the billing portal. Hypertask never shows internal IDs or the word "undefined". For customers without a team name in the app, the owner's email appears instead. Previously blank or malformatted names are now filled from the team name or owner email; customers that have neither team name nor matching owner remain blank.

> Verify customer names in your Stripe billing portal. If a name appears blank, check that its owning team has a name and that a matching owner email exists.

## Seats

Seats represent active users with individual access to Hypertask. Each seat corresponds to a user with login credentials and full access to the platform features.

**Seat limits by plan:**
- Free plan: Unlimited members and unlimited open tickets. You can own up to 3 boards. Archived boards are not counted. A paid or comped plan has no board limit.
- Paid and team plans: Active seat limits per plan
- Enterprise: Custom seat limits

When you create or add accounts, new seats are allocated automatically. Upgrading your paid plan increases your seat capacity; unrestricted reassignments are tracked for billing reconciliation.

## Cost forecasting

The cost forecast shows estimated consumption for GitHub repositories connected to Hypertask. This view helps you anticipate file storage and integration costs before they hit your budget.

**View your forecast:**
1. Go to the **Cost Forecast** page
2. See per-repository estimates broken down by usage type
3. Compare projections against your current subscriptions

## Testing billing changes safely

Stripe test-mode harness lets you safely test billing flows in production without risking database writes or production incidents.

The test harness:
- Runs **guarded seat billing logic** in a controlled environment
- Uses **in-memory application state** so tests don't affect live data
- Implements **bounded cleanup** to discard test states after execution
- **Never writes to the Hypertask database** during test runs

This means you can safely iterate on seat-loss logic, billing entitlement checks, and upgrade/downgrade flows in production-like conditions without creating cross-tenant leakage or corrupting live seats.

## Seat loss and automatic repair

Automatic repair of lost seats is available in production for affected teams. This feature prevents silent seat loss when users pool in from other teams, and helps maintain billing accuracy.

**How automatic repair works:**
- Detects when active teams have fewer seats than their current plan supports
- Verifies that the team has a valid Stripe payment method on file
- Requires billing-owner input if the active subscription cannot identify a single safe replacement Stripe item, to avoid modifying the wrong subscription item
- Blocks automatic repair and prompts for billing-owner review if:
  - A Stripe item is stored but no longer valid
  - The active subscription does not contain exactly one safe replacement at the stored price
  - Automatic selection could modify the wrong subscription item

Only teams with a payment method on file are eligible for automatic repair, and repair operations are guarded against unsafe mutations to subscriptions.

## License management

Seat allocation follows consistent rules across surfaces:

- New user creation adds a seat to your allocation
- Adding teammates in the app, via CLI, or through API all respect the same capacity checks
- Free plan members are unlimited
- Upgrading your plan increases your tracked capacity and adds seats automatically within the new tier bounds

## Team ownership verification

All billing-affected endpoints now verify team ownership server-side before performing mutations:

| Endpoint | Change |
|----------|--------|
| Checkout session creation | Verifies the authenticated user has billing access to the team before creating a checkout URL |
| Task mutations | Reads billing authority from the authenticated user and enforces access checks before state changes |
| Comment operations | Validates the requesting user's access to the target board and task before posting |

This prevents client-controlled parameter mismatches from bypassing authorization and ensures operations are scoped only to the intended team's resources.

## Stripe customer operations

Stripe customer creation for new accounts now surfaces all errors rather than silently swallowing them. Previously, certain paths returned null on failure without indicating the underlying issue, making debugging difficult. All customer creation paths now properly report errors to help you identify and resolve account or payment configuration problems.

Claude Haiku 5.5 has been released as the new default AI model for everyone, replacing Haiku 4.5. The change brings consistent model behavior across all AI surfaces including AI Task Writer, Agent Chat, and code-generation workflows.

**Model choice and behavior:**
- Haiku 5.5 now serves as the default model for all new AI conversations
- The replacement reduces confusion around having multiple Haiku versions live simultaneously
- Model quality reflects real-world usage patterns and usage-based cost

**Real-world cost:**
In live measurements on the QA Sandbox board, Claude Haiku 5.5 costs approximately 1.7x more per request than GPT 6 Luna. This difference stems from longer answer lengths rather than per-token pricing parity:

```
AI chat, 10 prompts each on the same board:
- Haiku 5.5: 1.70x cost of GPT 6 Luna per request
- All models use identical per-token pricing
```

The model is fully operational on all supported environments including Free and paid subscription tiers.

When Haiku 5.5 is selected (or left as default), it behaves equivalently to GPT 6 Luna in all supported AI workflows, ensuring predictable outputs regardless of model provider.

---
title: Smart Labels
description: Labels with an AI prompt that automatically stay assigned to matching tasks — soft, prompt-defined views.
---


A **smart label** is a label with an AI prompt attached. The AI reads each task and keeps the label assigned to the ones that match your prompt — so a filter or saved view on that label becomes a **prompt-defined view** ("show me small quick wins", "everything touching billing") instead of a hard filter.

## Creating a smart label

<Steps>

1. Open the label modal on a task (or the Manage Tags screen) and type a new label name.

2. Fill the **"Smart label — AI keeps this label on matching tasks"** field with a plain-language description of which tasks belong, e.g. `Small, low-risk changes shippable in under an hour`.

3. Save. The AI immediately classifies the board's existing tasks (up to 500) and labels the matches. Smart labels show a sparkle icon in label lists.

</Steps>

## How it stays current

- **New tasks** are classified when created.
- **Edited tasks** are re-classified when their title or description changes.
- **Prompt changes** re-run classification for the whole board.

Label changes made by the AI appear in the task's activity feed as HyperAI.

<Aside type="note">
The latest AI verdict wins: if you manually add or remove a smart label on a task, the AI may reverse it the next time that task is re-classified. Describe exceptions in the prompt instead ("NOT: schema changes").
</Aside>

## Using it as a view

Filter the board by the smart label (or save that filter as a view) and you have a Kanban/table that only shows AI-matched tasks.

## Details

- Prompts are capped at 1000 characters; setting one requires project membership.
- Classification runs on a fast, low-cost model; usage is logged like other AI features.
- Backfill covers the 500 oldest tasks per run; newer activity is always classified.
- The parser tolerates extra text around the list of labels that the model returns, so smart labels classify more reliably and show fewer parsing errors.
